nodes.label: RoutingStrategy
nodes.rationale: (routees, state) => Iterable<ActorRef>, where state carries only the monotonic message index. The local router ships four implementations plus a custom slot; the cluster router has a counterpart for each and adds consistent-hashing.

nodes.label: Round-robin strategy
nodes.rationale: Even distribution by message COUNT, deterministic and inspectable. It does not load-balance by work cost - the router does not know a message is heavy - and gives no 'stick to the same routee' guarantee. The right default for homogeneous workloads.

nodes.label: Random strategy
nodes.rationale: Same long-run distribution as round-robin but with no shared state, and more resilient to synchronized senders that would otherwise hammer the same routees. It gives up deterministic test behavior - inject a seedable RNG in a custom strategy if reproducibility matters.

nodes.label: Broadcast strategy
nodes.rationale: N-way fan-out with N-way work: cache invalidation, periodic refresh, heartbeats. It does not parallelize work - every routee does the same work - and makes no sense for request/response, where the caller sees N replies. For occasional fan-out, keep the router non-broadcast and wrap the message in Broadcast<T>.

nodes.label: Smallest-mailbox strategy
nodes.rationale: The only built-in strategy that reacts to what routees are actually doing: it balances by backlog rather than by turn, is self-correcting after a stall (a blocked routee drains no queue, so it simply stops being chosen - no timer, no health check), and rotates ties. Costs an O(N) scan per message, knows count not cost, and applies no back-pressure, because a strategy that refused to route would be inventing back-pressure the caller never configured.

nodes.label: What counts as a depth
nodes.rationale: Two unusable cases handled as opposites. A stopped routee is never chosen: its mailbox is permanently empty because a terminated cell dead-letters instead of enqueueing, so read as a plain number it would be the most attractive member of the pool until the router learns of the death - a window as deep as the router's own queue under load. A routee whose depth is merely unreadable counts as EMPTY, because skipping it would starve a remote routee for as long as any local one has a backlog; a balance error corrects itself, starvation does not.

nodes.label: Cluster smallest-mailbox on cached depths
nodes.rationale: A remote routee's mailbox is not readable from here and asking per message would park the router's whole mailbox behind a network round-trip, so each node's depth is cached and refreshed on a background tick while routing reads the cache synchronously. Consequences: a depth can be one refresh interval stale so a node may be chosen just after filling up, and a node that has not reported is skipped rather than assumed idle.

nodes.label: Consistent-hashing (cluster only)
nodes.rationale: Rendezvous hashing on extractKey(message): same key, same routee, deterministically across the cluster, so a routee can maintain per-key state without a coordinator. Topology-stable - adding or removing a routee reshuffles only a 1/N fraction of keys. It does not balance skewed keys, and does not pin hard; for that use a singleton or a sharded entity.

nodes.label: Custom strategies
nodes.rationale: A custom strategy sees only the routee refs and the message index and must carry any other state in a closure. Notably it cannot reach mailbox depth: that is runtime-internal state and deliberately not on ActorRef, so a load-aware strategy of your own would need routees reporting into a shared gauge - which is why the built-in smallestMailbox reads it from inside the framework where the state legitimately lives.

nodes.label: Aside claiming actor-ts ships no scatter-gather router
nodes.rationale: This page's caution says actor-ts does not ship a scatter-gather router and that you would build one as a custom router actor - but Router.scatterGatherFirstCompleted is documented as a shipped sixth factory on its own page and in routing/overview and router. Flagged as an apparent stale/contradictory statement for review rather than omitted.
